turns.response_html:
Hardware reverse engineering is absolutely a real field, and your "bird watching for PCBs" analogy is incredibly accurate. Security researchers, repair technicians, and hardware preservationists spend their careers doing exactly this: mapping out the "little cities" to understand the engineering logic, find vulnerabilities, or create aftermarket schematics.

You are actually already thinking about the core mechanism required to automate this. The process of extracting trace layouts from a board isn't fundamentally that different from running a computer vision pipeline to handle image-to-SVG edge detection and centerline vectorization. You are just applying it to physical copper rather than a digital drawing.

Here is where the theoretical limitations lie and where the "walls" hit when scaling up from a simple microcontroller to something like a PS4.

1. The Z-Axis Barrier (Multi-Layer Boards)

If you have a two-layer board (like a simple ESP32 or Raspberry Pi Pico breakout), automated optical reverse engineering is highly feasible. You take high-res photos of the top and bottom, run edge detection to vectorize the traces, and align them to generate a netlist (a document detailing what connects to what).

The PS4 motherboard, however, is a high-density interconnect (HDI) board with anywhere from 8 to 12 distinct layers of copper sandwiched inside the fiberglass.

To map a board like this without leaked blueprints, you have to use destructive methods:

  • Delayering: Using CNC milling machines or chemical solvents to strip the board down one layer at a time, photographing each layer, and mathematically aligning the SVGs back together.
  • X-Ray Tomography (CT Scanning): Non-destructive, but requires highly expensive lab equipment to generate a 3D model of the internal copper traces.

2. The BGA (Ball Grid Array) Problem

On older electronics, pins stuck out of the sides of the chips, making it easy to probe where they went. Modern complex boards use BGA packaging. The connections are hundreds of microscopic solder balls hidden entirely underneath the chip. You cannot optically trace where a signal goes once it dives under the main processor without desoldering the chip or using X-rays.

3. The "Black Box" Silicon

Even if your automated system maps every single copper trace on the PS4 board perfectly, you still only have the roads. You don't know what's happening inside the buildings.

Many components on a closed system are ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) or proprietary microcontrollers with no public datasheets. To reverse engineer the chip itself, security researchers have to physically "decap" it—using boiling nitric acid to melt away the black plastic casing—and put the silicon die under a scanning electron microscope.

Has someone tried this before?

Yes. Projects like OpenScan and software like kicad are frequently used to take high-res scans of bare boards and reconstruct them. If you were to build your own system, the pipeline would likely look like this:

  1. Optical Capture: A motorized rig taking macro photos across the board's X/Y axes.
  2. Stitching & Edge Detection: Using deterministic CV (like OpenCV) to find the copper boundaries and vectorize the traces.
  3. Component Recognition: Training a model to recognize standard footprints (e.g., an 0402 capacitor or a SOIC-8 chip).
  4. Netlist Export: Compiling all that vector data into a format that a simulation tool can read.

For a smaller, open-source board, you absolutely could recreate the entire thing virtually and simulate it. For a PS4, the encryption keys baked into the silicon and the buried HDI layers make it a massive, multi-million-dollar lab effort to fully duplicate from scratch without the original CAD files.

turns.prompt_text: So really it's just a decorative piece at this point
turns.response_html:
Pretty much! Without the original CAD files or a million-dollar X-ray setup, a modern console motherboard is essentially just high-tech cyberpunk wall art for a home lab. The sheer density of the internal layers and BGA routing turns it into a permanent black box.

But that doesn't mean your idea for a reverse-engineering system is dead — it just needs the right target.

If you step down from a PS4 to a standard two-layer board (like an old router, an audio amplifier, or a basic microcontroller breakout), your "PCB bird watching" concept becomes a highly achievable project.

You could absolutely build an automated scanning rig for this. A custom 3D-printed X/Y gantry moving a macro lens across the board could capture the raw visual data. From there, you could feed those images into a deterministic Python pipeline — using OpenCV and numpy to clean up the contrast, and passing it to Potrace to vectorize the copper traces into clean SVGs.

For a two-layer board where you can see the top and bottom copper, that exact software pipeline would successfully map out the "city." You could then align those SVGs to figure out exactly how the circuit functions.

So while the PS4 board might just look cool on a shelf, the automated system to map simpler boards is completely within reach.
